claim: Cross frequency coupling (CFC) is emerging as a fundamental feature of brain activity, correlated with brain function and dysfunction.
source: Cross frequency coupling (CFC) is emerging as a fundamental feature of brain activity, correlated with brain function and dysfunction.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract without specific data or citations provided in this sentence.

claim: Many different types of CFC have been identified through application of numerous data analysis methods, each developed to characterize a specific CFC type.
source: Many different types of CFC have been identified through application of numerous data analysis methods, each developed to characterize a specific CFC type.
evidence: This statement refers to established knowledge in the field about CFC analysis methods.

claim: Choosing an inappropriate method weakens statistical power and introduces opportunities for confounding effects.
source: Choosing an inappropriate method weakens statistical power and introduces opportunities for confounding effects.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of method selection.

claim: The proposed method successfully detects CFC between the low frequency phase or amplitude and the high frequency amplitude in simulations.
source: We show in simulations that the proposed method successfully detects CFC between the low frequency phase or amplitude and the high frequency amplitude
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The proposed method outperforms an existing method in biologically-motivated examples.
source: We show in simulations that the proposed method successfully detects CFC between the low frequency phase or amplitude and the high frequency amplitude, and outperforms an existing method in biologically-motivated examples.
evidence: This is supported by comparative simulation data in the manuscript.

claim: Brain rhythms play a critical role in coordinating brain networks.
source: Brain rhythms - as recorded in the local field potential (LFP) or scalp electroencephalogram (EEG) - are believed to play a critical role in coordinating brain networks.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific belief without specific citation in this sentence.

claim: Rhythmic fluctuations provide an effective means to control the timing of neuronal firing by modulating neural excitability.
source: By modulating neural excitability, these rhythmic fluctuations provide an effective means to control the timing of neuronal firing (Engel et al., 2001; Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The theta band is associated with memory, plasticity, and navigation.
source: the theta band with memory, plasticity, and navigation (Engel et al., 2001)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The gamma band is associated with local coupling and competition.
source: the gamma band with local coupling and competition (Kopell et al., 2000; Börgers et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Gamma and high-gamma (80–200 Hz) activity have been identified as surrogate markers of neuronal firing.
source: In addition, gamma and high-gamma (80–200 Hz) activity have been identified as surrogate markers of neuronal firing (Rasch et al., 2008; Mukamel et al., 2005; Fries et al., 2001; Pesaran et al., 2002; Whittingstall and Logothetis, 2009; Ray and Maunsell, 2011)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Lower frequency rhythms engage larger brain areas and modulate spatially localized fast activity.
source: In general, lower frequency rhythms engage larger brain areas and modulate spatially localized fast activity (Bragin et al., 1995; Chrobak and Buzsáki, 1998; von Stein and Sarnthein, 2000; Lakatos et al., 2005; Lakatos et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The phase of low frequency rhythms has been shown to modulate and coordinate neural spiking.
source: For example, the phase of low frequency rhythms has been shown to modulate and coordinate neural spiking (Vinck et al., 2010; Hyafil et al., 2015b; Fries et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: CFC has been shown to carry behaviorally relevant information related to position, memory, decision making and coordination.
source: This particular type of CFC has been shown to carry behaviorally relevant information (e.g., related to position [Jensen and Lisman, 2000; Agarwal et al., 2014], memory [Siegel et al., 2009], decision making and coordination [Dean et al., 2012; Pesaran et al., 2008; Wong et al., 2016; Hawellek et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: CFC has been observed in many brain areas.
source: More generally, CFC has been observed in many brain areas (Bragin et al., 1995; Chrobak and Buzsáki, 1998; Csicsvari et al., 2003; Tort et al., 2008; Mormann et al., 2005; Canolty et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: CFC has been linked to specific circuit and dynamical mechanisms.
source: CFC has been observed in many brain areas (Bragin et al., 1995; Chrobak and Buzsáki, 1998; Csicsvari et al., 2003; Tort et al., 2008; Mormann et al., 2005; Canolty et al., 2006), and linked to specific circuit and dynamical mechanisms (Hyafil et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The degree of CFC has been linked to working memory, neuronal computation, communication, learning and emotion.
source: The degree of CFC in those areas has been linked to working memory, neuronal computation, communication, learning and emotion (Tort et al., 2009; Jensen et al., 2016; Canolty and Knight, 2010; Dejean et al., 2016; Karalis et al., 2016; Likhtik et al., 2014; Jones and Wilson, 2005; Lisman, 2005; Sirota et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: CFC has been linked to clinical disorders including epilepsy.
source: The degree of CFC in those areas has been linked to working memory, neuronal computation, communication, learning and emotion (Tort et al., 2009; Jensen et al., 2016; Canolty and Knight, 2010; Dejean et al., 2016; Karalis et al., 2016; Likhtik et al., 2014; Jones and Wilson, 2005; Lisman, 2005; Sirota et al., 2008), and clinical disorders (Gordon, 2016; Widge et al., 2017; Voytek and Knight, 2015; Başar et al., 2016; Mathalon and Sohal, 2015), including epilepsy (Weiss et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The neuronal substrate of CFC itself remains obscure.
source: Although the cellular mechanisms giving rise to some neural rhythms are relatively well understood (e.g. gamma [Whittington et al., 2000; Whittington et al., 2011; Mann and Mody, 2010]), the neuronal substrate of CFC itself remains obscure.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The notion of CFC subsumes more specific types of coupling, including phase-phase coupling (PPC), phase-amplitude coupling (PAC), and amplitude-amplitude coupling (AAC).
source: The notion of CFC, therefore, subsumes more specific types of coupling, including: phase-phase coupling (PPC), phase-amplitude coupling (PAC), and amplitude-amplitude coupling (AAC) (Hyafil et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: PAC has been observed in rodent striatum and hippocampus.
source: PAC has been observed in rodent striatum and hippocampus (Tort et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: PAC has been observed in human cortex.
source: PAC has been observed in rodent striatum and hippocampus (Tort et al., 2008) and human cortex (Canolty et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: AAC has been observed between the alpha and gamma rhythms in dorsal and ventral cortices.
source: AAC has been observed between the alpha and gamma rhythms in dorsal and ventral cortices (Popov et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: AAC has been observed between theta and gamma rhythms during spatial navigation.
source: AAC has been observed between the alpha and gamma rhythms in dorsal and ventral cortices (Popov et al., 2018), and between theta and gamma rhythms during spatial navigation (Shirvalkar et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Both PAC and AAC have been observed between alpha and gamma rhythms.
source: both PAC and AAC have been observed between alpha and gamma rhythms (Osipova et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Changes in the low frequency power can affect measures of PAC.
source: Changes in the low frequency power can also affect measures of PAC; increases in low frequency power can increase the signal to noise ratio of phase and amplitude variables, increasing the measure of PAC, even when the phase-amplitude coupling remains constant (Aru et al., 2015; van Wijk et al., 2015; Jensen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Increases in low frequency power can increase the signal to noise ratio of phase and amplitude variables, increasing the measure of PAC, even when the phase-amplitude coupling remains constant.
source: Changes in the low frequency power can also affect measures of PAC; increases in low frequency power can increase the signal to noise ratio of phase and amplitude variables, increasing the measure of PAC, even when the phase-amplitude coupling remains constant (Aru et al., 2015; van Wijk et al., 2015; Jensen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: An accurate measure of PAC would control for confounding variables, including the power of low frequency oscillations.
source: These observations suggest that an accurate measure of PAC would control for confounding variables, including the power of low frequency oscillations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observations about confounding effects.

claim: The proposed generalized linear model (GLM) framework assesses CFC between the high-frequency amplitude and, simultaneously, the low frequency phase and amplitude.
source: To that end, we propose here a generalized linear model (GLM) framework to assess CFC between the high-frequency amplitude and, simultaneously, the low frequency phase and amplitude.
evidence: This describes the method proposed in the manuscript.

claim: The proposed framework builds upon previous work.
source: This formal statistical inference framework builds upon previous work (Kramer and Eden, 2013; Penny et al., 2008; Voytek et al., 2013; van Wijk et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The proposed method more accurately detects PAC than the modulation index in signals with CFC dependent on the low-frequency amplitude.
source: We compare this method to the modulation index, and show that in signals with CFC dependent on the low-frequency amplitude, the proposed method more accurately detects PAC than the modulation index.
evidence: This is supported by comparative simulation data in the manuscript.

claim: The gamma distribution provides an acceptable fit to the example human data analyzed.
source: We choose this distribution as it guarantees real, positive amplitude values; we note that this distribution provides an acceptable fit to the example human data analyzed here (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1 showing the fit.

claim: Two deviance-based model comparison procedures for GLMs are less robust measures of significant PAC and AAC than R_PAC and R_AAC.
source: We conclude that, in this modeling regime, two deviance-based model comparison procedures for GLMs are less robust measures of significant PAC and AAC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative simulation results.

claim: In three BLA-IL pairings from rodent data, the amplitude of the low frequency IL signal increases from pre- to post-stimulation.
source: Investigating further, we note that in all three cases, the amplitude of the low frequency IL signal increases from pre- to post-stimulation
evidence: This is supported by analysis of in vivo rodent data.

claim: The increase in MI observed in rodent data may result from changes in the low frequency amplitude and AAC, not in PAC.
source: We therefore propose that, consistent with these simulation results, the increase in MI observed in these data may result from changes in the low frequency amplitude and AAC, not in PAC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data analysis and simulation results.

claim: There is evidence for a significant effect of stimulus on PAC in the example rodent data.
source: Hence, we find evidence for a significant effect of stimulus on PAC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The method effectively determines whether stimulation condition significantly changes PAC.
source: We conclude that this method effectively determines whether stimulation condition significantly changes PAC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the simulation results.

claim: The proposed method is more sensitive to weak PAC obscured by or coupled to low-frequency amplitude fluctuations.
source: We have shown that this method effectively detects CFC, both as PAC and AAC, and is more sensitive to weak PAC obscured by or coupled to low-frequency amplitude fluctuations.
evidence: This is a summary of the results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The simultaneous occurrence of PAC and AAC is less well studied than PAC alone.
source: While PAC often occurs in neural data, and has been associated with numerous neurological functions (Canolty and Knight, 2010; Hyafil et al., 2015b), the simultaneous occurrence of PAC and AAC is less well studied (Osipova et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: High frequency rhythms provide a surrogate measure of neuronal spiking.
source: Low frequency rhythms are associated with the aggregate activity of large neural populations and modulations of neuronal excitability (Engel et al., 2001; Varela et al., 2001; Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004), while high frequency rhythms provided a surrogate measure of neuronal spiking (Rasch et al., 2008; Mukamel et al., 2005; Fries et al., 2001; Pesaran et al., 2002; Whittingstall and Logothetis, 2009; Ray and Maunsell, 2011; Ray et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The function of concurrent PAC and AAC, both for healthy brain function and during a seizure, is not well understood.
source: The function of concurrent PAC and AAC, both for healthy brain function and during a seizure as illustrated here, is not well understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Proposed functions of PAC include multi-item encoding, long-distance communication, and sensory parsing.
source: Proposed functions of PAC include multi-item encoding, long-distance communication, and sensory parsing (Hyafil et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A proposed function of AAC is to encode the number of represented items, or the amount of information encoded in the modulated signal.
source: Similarly, a proposed function of AAC is to encode the number of represented items, or the amount of information encoded in the modulated signal (Hyafil et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A pathological increase in AAC may support the transmission of more information than is needed, overloading the communication of relevant information with irrelevant noise.
source: A pathological increase in AAC may support the transmission of more information than is needed, overloading the communication of relevant information with irrelevant noise.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential function of AAC.

claim: The attention-based function of PAC may be lost if the amplitude of the high frequency oscillation is increased across wide intervals of low frequency phase.
source: The attention-based function of PAC, that is having reduced high frequency amplitude at phases not containing the targeted information, may be lost if the amplitude of the high frequency oscillation is increased across wide intervals of low frequency phase.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential consequences of increased high frequency amplitude.

claim: If the wrong frequency bands are chosen, coupling may be missed.
source: Hence, if the wrong frequency bands are chosen, coupling may be missed.
evidence: This is an inference about the consequences of incorrect frequency band selection.

claim: The proposed modeling framework assumes the data contain approximately sinusoidal signals, which have been appropriately isolated for analysis.
source: Fourth, we note that the proposed modeling framework assumes the data contain approximately sinusoidal signals, which have been appropriately isolated for analysis.
evidence: This is a statement about an assumption of the method.

claim: CFC measures are sensitive to non-sinusoidal signals, which may confound interpretation of cross-frequency analyses.
source: In general, CFC measures are sensitive to non-sinusoidal signals, which may confound interpretation of cross-frequency analyses (Cole and Voytek, 2017; Kramer et al., 2008; Aru et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The proposed method can easily be extended by inclusion of additional predictors in the GLM.
source: The proposed method can easily be extended by inclusion of additional predictors in the GLM.
evidence: This is a statement about the flexibility of the method.

claim: The code developed to implement the method is flexible and modular, which facilitates modifications and extensions.
source: The code developed to implement the method is flexible and modular, which facilitates modifications and extensions motivated by the particular data analysis scenario.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of the code.

claim: The code is freely available for reuse and further development at https://github.com/Eden-Kramer-Lab/GLM-CFC.
source: This modular code, available at https://github.com/Eden-Kramer-Lab/GLM-CFC, also allows the user to change latent assumptions, such as choice of frequency bands and filtering method. The code is freely available for reuse and further development.
evidence: This is a statement about code availability.
